opus-5.5.text:
Sure. When most people evaluate an AI model, they look at it from the outside: you give it an input, check the output, and summarize everything with one number, like the loss or the accuracy on a benchmark. That is a very coarse view. It's like describing a whole city by its average temperature.

Coming from physics, my instinct is to zoom in. A neural network is not a homogeneous blob. It has layers, neurons, attention heads, weights connecting particular units. Different parts of that space do different jobs. Some regions handle syntax, some store facts, some do something that looks like arithmetic. If you only look at the global behavior, all of that structure gets averaged away.

So by "looking more finely across space," I mean resolving the model spatially, the way a physicist might go from thermodynamics down to individual particles, or a biologist from the whole organism down to brain regions. You ask: where in the network does this computation happen? Is it localized or spread out? Are there modules? How do information and representations flow from one part to another?

That's also why in some of my work, like the brain-inspired modular training idea, I tried to give neurons an actual geometric layout and penalize long-range connections. Once the network has a notion of space and locality, modules naturally emerge and you can literally see the circuit. It becomes much more interpretable, the way a well-organized city is easier to navigate than a random tangle of roads.

And there's a parallel idea across time. You can look at how these spatial structures form during training, not just at the final model. Put the two together, a fine-grained picture across both space and time, and I think we get much closer to actually understanding these systems as scientific objects, rather than just measuring how well they perform.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts input-output evaluation with examining internal structure, including layers, neurons, attention heads, and where computations occur.

fable-5.1.text:
So when I say "looking more finely across space," I'm really contrasting it with how most people look at neural networks, which is at the level of the whole model, or at best at the level of a layer. You train a transformer, you measure the loss, you look at scaling curves. That's a very coarse view. Everything inside is treated as a black box, and the only thing you see is the aggregate behavior.

What I mean by finer spatial resolution is going inside and asking: what is each individual component doing? Not "what does layer twelve do," but "what does this particular neuron, or this particular attention head, or even this particular weight, contribute?" Because a neural network is a physical object in some sense. It has a geometry. There are weights laid out in matrices, there are activations flowing through specific paths, and when you zoom in you find that the computation isn't uniformly spread out. It's localized. Certain neurons fire for very specific features, certain heads implement very specific circuits, and a lot of the network is actually doing very little.

This is actually where a lot of my physics background comes in. In physics, when we want to understand a material, we don't just measure its bulk properties, like how conductive it is. We look at the microstructure. We look at where the atoms are, how they're arranged, where defects are. And the macroscopic properties emerge from that microscopic structure. I think of neural networks the same way. If you want to really understand why a model generalizes, or why grokking happens, or why some training runs succeed and others fail, you can't just stare at the loss curve. You have to look at what's happening at the level of individual units and how they're organized spatially.

And a concrete example of this is the work on KANs, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks. One motivation there was precisely to make the model more interpretable at the fine-grained level, where each edge of the network carries a learnable one-dimensional function that you can actually plot and look at. So instead of a huge weight matrix where every number is meaningless on its own, you have a structure where you can point at a specific piece and say, this piece is computing a sine, this piece is computing a square. The spatial fineness is built into the architecture.

So "finer across space" is really about resolution. Instead of a blurry picture of the whole model, you want a sharp picture of its parts. And once you have that, I think a lot of the mysteries about why these systems work start to look less mysterious, because you can actually trace the mechanism.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts aggregate views such as loss and whole-model behavior with examining internal components, including individual neurons, heads, and weights.

astra-6.text: By looking more finely across space, I mean looking inside the model at its different parts, rather than treating the whole model as a single black box. You can measure its overall performance, but that doesn’t tell you what individual layers, neurons, or connections are doing. So you zoom in and ask: Where is a particular computation happening? How do these components work together? It’s like studying the brain—you can look at behavior, but you can also look at brain regions and individual neurons. Those different levels of detail can give you different kinds of understanding.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts examining the model’s internal parts with treating it as a black box and measuring only its overall performance.

sol-6.1.text: By looking more finely across space, I mean looking inside the model instead of treating it as one big black box. You can study it at the level of layers, then individual neurons or connections, and ask what each part is doing. Which parts respond to a particular feature? How do those parts work together to produce an answer? It’s like increasing the resolution of a microscope: the overall behavior is still important, but you’re trying to see the smaller structures that give rise to it.

r001.rationale: It contrasts studying the model’s internal layers, neurons, and connections with treating it as one black box, while distinguishing that from overall behavior.
